items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Names like `pending`, `worker`, `cancelled_again` and `remaining` say what they hold. The docstring states the cancellation and error behaviour, and the less obvious steps have comments ("Wait for every worker to finish its cleanup, even if we get cancelled again"). The only single-letter name is `w`, used as a loop variable.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: It builds its own machinery instead of the TaskGroup the project conventions ask for: a `nonlocal stop` flag, a hand-written cancel/`while remaining:` re-wait loop and manual exception retrieval. That puts about 50 lines in one function where TaskGroup plus a Semaphore would take a few.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: `if max_concurrent < 1: raise ValueError`. It re-raises the first worker exception and cancels and awaits the other workers in `finally`. It catches only `asyncio.CancelledError` during cleanup and re-raises it afterwards, so nothing is swallowed. It also retrieves worker exceptions so asyncio doesn't log "never retrieved".

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: `if not tasks: return`; `max_concurrent < 1` raises ValueError. On FIRST_EXCEPTION it re-raises the error, and `finally` sets `stop = True`, cancels the workers and awaits them, so cleanup runs and queued tasks never start. No worker task is left orphaned.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: `async def run_tasks(tasks: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]], max_concurrent: int) -> None`. Each worker calls `job = next(pending)` and then `await job()` only when it has a free slot, so every callable is invoked lazily, at most once. It uses only the standard library, and importing the module runs nothing.
